The idea is a short-horizon reversal: yesterday's return is bearish, so the factor is minus yesterday's return. I'll start with the plainest form — negative 1-day return — to see how much survives once the short-term reversal style is removed.

The idea says closing near the day's high is bullish, so I'll measure each day's close position inside the day's high–low range — a ratio of close to high, which is unit-free and comparable across coins — and average it over a 5-day window with the positive sign the idea implies.

What I found: the idea holds up on this history. Each day's close position inside the day's high–low range, averaged over 5 days, gives an incremental IC of +0.0210 with t = 8.7 and the same positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so coins closing near their high do tend to outperform. The effect is clearly weaker when the window is lengthened to 20 days, which suggests the signal is short-lived.

What I found: measuring how far a coin closes above its open each day and averaging over 5 days gives essentially no incremental information — the incremental IC is −0.0003 with a t of −1.3, and the raw rank IC is −0.04, meaning the "close far above open" shape is mostly a repackaged short-term reversal signal. Smoothing over 20 days made it worse, so this idea does not hold on this history in its stated direction. I keep the direction the idea specifies (higher close above open → higher factor value), and hand in the simple 5-day mean of the shape.

But almost all of that is already captured by the known styles (liquidity), leaving only 0.0011 incremental, and the incremental IC flips sign slightly in 2024, so the effect is weak and unstable. Compressing the log of dollar volume or stretching the window to 60 days both hurt, so the plain level of dollar volume is the best and most faithful form of the idea.
